claims.text: The baseline material is a high-entropy-alloy protective coating containing a standard amount of a reactive element such as Cr or Al and applied to a substrate.
Reactive-element content will be varied above and below the baseline by a few weight percent.
A nanoscale tribo-layer forms on the coating surface during sliding wear.
Increasing Cr or Al content increases chemical reactivity at the sliding interface.
Increasing reactive-element content accelerates formation of the tribo-layer.
Increasing reactive-element content makes the tribo-layer more stable.
The protective tribo-layer may consist of an oxide or a similar compound.
Formation of a protective oxide tribo-layer can reduce wear.
Formation of the tribo-layer reduces the coefficient of friction.
The tribo-layer functions as a self-healing barrier during wear.
Coatings with increased reactive-element content will have a more continuous and stable tribo-layer than the baseline coating.
Coatings with increased reactive-element content will have lower wear volume than the baseline coating.
Coatings with increased reactive-element content will have a lower coefficient of friction than the baseline coating.
Reducing reactive-element content will impair tribo-layer formation and increase wear.
The baseline composition has a less developed tribo-layer and a higher wear rate than compositions with increased reactive-element content.
The proposed composition–tribo-layer–wear relationship should hold for reactive-element changes of a few weight percent under ambient, room-temperature sliding conditions.
Its applicability under very high temperatures or extreme mechanical loads is untested.
Other alloying elements and resulting microstructural changes may affect the magnitude of the wear response.
Absence of systematic changes in tribo-layer characteristics, wear rate, or friction with reactive-element content would falsify the hypothesis.
